minutes.headline: Commissioners approved three warrant articles for the Feb. 25 special town meeting, including funds for a new excavator
minutes.summary: The Water District Commissioners voted to send three warrant articles to a February 25 special meeting -- an IRS pass-through payment, a Neptune data-collector gateway, and a rubber tire excavator -- and delayed the FY2025 audit review and the PFAS financing survey rollout. Much of the meeting was spent responding to public criticism and Facebook posts about the PFAS/hard-water treatment plan and survey, with commissioners defending their process and a resident from a citizens' clean-water group pressing for a full multi-well treatment plan and cost comparisons before residents are asked to vote.

what_happened.line: Commissioners voted to send three warrant articles — an IRS pass-through payment, a Neptune meter-reading gateway, and a replacement excavator — to the Feb. 25 special district meeting.
A resident confirmed the roughly an amount as heard total for the three articles comes from the surplus revenue account, not a tax override.
The board postponed rollout of its PFAS/hard-water treatment financing survey a week, pending clarity on whether the state loan program's interest rate is 0% or 2%.
Much of the meeting was spent answering public criticism of the PFAS survey process, with a resident pressing for a full multi-well treatment plan and cost comparisons before any vote.
The current state loan (SRF) application covers only two wells; a third, Keating's, was left out for lack of completed pilot data and may be added later by addendum.

why_it_matters: The three warrant articles go to voters at the Feb. 25 special district meeting and are funded from surplus, not a tax override.

The PFAS/hard-water treatment financing survey — which shapes what residents may later be asked to fund — was held back while the state clarifies its loan interest rate, so any cost estimate shown to residents depends on that rate.
The state loan application now covers two of the district's wells, not three, which affects how much of any eventual treatment cost could be offset by subsidized financing.
